label: explain_concept
text:
During LLM inference, the model generates one token at a time. Attention at each step needs the key and value vectors of every earlier token. Those vectors depend only on tokens already produced, so they stay fixed as new tokens arrive.

KV caching stores those key and value tensors after the first pass. On the next step the model computes query, key, and value only for the new token, then attends over the stored history plus that new token. The prompt is processed once. Later steps reuse the cache and append one new key-value pair.

This avoids repeating work as the sequence grows. The cost is memory: the cache grows with sequence length, batch size, layers, and attention heads, so long contexts consume a lot of GPU memory.

raw.thought:
I will explain KV caching in LLM inference to a junior developer in about 120 words.

KV caching stores the key and value vectors from earlier tokens. During autoregressive generation, these vectors never change. Without caching, the entire sequence would be recomputed on every new token.

With KV caching, only the query vector is computed for each new token. The cached keys and values are reused across all subsequent steps.

The prompt is processed once. Later steps append only a new query-key-value pair. This avoids redundant work as the sequence grows. The tradeoff is memory: the cache scales with sequence length, batch size, layers, and heads.
